1The Poisson approximation at work: five dice rolled 2000 times

The lecture opens by finishing the example started at the end of Lecture 10 (the Poisson distribution as a limit of the binomial).

Example

On a single roll of 5 dice, the probability that all 5 dice show the same value is

You plan on rolling the 5 dice 2000 times and will let count the number the number of times all 5 dice show the same value.

“the number the number” is repeated on the board, as transcribed.

Next board:

We can estimate probabilities associated with by using a Poisson random variable .

Do we get good estimates?

✎ Explanation (added)

Where comes from. “All five the same” is six disjoint outcomes: all 1s, all 2s, …, all 6s. Each one has probability because the dice are independent, and the addition rule for disjoint events adds the six: . A quicker way to see it: the first die can show anything, and the other four must match it, .

Why is binomial. Each of the 2000 rolls is a trial with two outcomes (all the same or not), the rolls are independent, and on every roll. counts successes, so (Lecture 9).

Why Poisson. The two checks are the Lecture 10 conditions: and . The Poisson parameter is the binomial mean, , so we expect about one and a half “all the same” rolls in 2000. (Lecture 10’s board wrote the second condition as ; here it is . Either way, passes.)

2Probability as a fraction of area

Chapter 4 starts with a question about choosing a point at random.

Question

If all points in the following square are equally likely to be selected, and we divide the square into 4 equal sized quadrants, what is the probability we choose a point in the upper right quadrant?

Answer:  (look at the fraction of the square’s area occupied by the upper right quadrant).

✎ Explanation (added)

In Lecture 4, equally likely outcomes gave classical probability : count the outcomes in the event and divide by the count of all outcomes. A square has infinitely many points, so counting fails. The fix is to measure instead of count: replace “number of points” by “area”, so

The upper right quadrant is a quarter of the square whatever the square’s size, so the answer is . This is the idea the rest of the lecture builds on.

Question

Total area under the curve is .

If you randomly select a point in the region between the curve and the axis and all points are equally likely to be selected, what is the probability you choose a point in the shaded region?

Answer: , the fraction of the area occupied by the shaded region.

The next board adds the key special case:

* If the area of the region between the curve and the axis is 1  , then the probability you select a point in the shaded region is just the area of the shaded region

Not content: in the first photo of this board the instructor’s arm is at the left edge, and “448” at the bottom looks like leftover writing, not part of the question. The third photo has faint words from an erased board on the right.

✎ Explanation (added)

This is the square question again with a curved region. “Equally likely” still means probability is a fraction of area, now (shaded area)/(total area) .

The starred line is why every density curve in this chapter has total area 1. When the division disappears and probability is just area. Lecture 7’s density histogram for a pmf was built the same way: bar areas were probabilities and they added to 1.

Textbook Devore does not use “pick a random point under the curve”. It reaches the same picture another way: a probability histogram of lake depth, measured more and more finely, with total area 1, approaches a smooth curve (§4.1, p. 143, Figure 4.1).

3A random variable built from the area under a curve

Example

Suppose is positive on the interval and the area under the curve on this interval is .

Let’s create a random variable that assigns a value to a chosen point that is equal to its coordinate.

If you choose the point , assigns the value to this point.

A short word before “chosen” is scribbled out on the board.

✎ Explanation (added)

This is the Lecture 7 definition of a random variable: a rule that assigns a number to each outcome. The outcome is a point chosen at random from the region of area 1, and the rule keeps the coordinate and throws away.

Many points have the same coordinate: the whole vertical segment from the axis up to the curve. Where the curve is tall that segment is long, so values of near there are more likely. That is why will be called a density: its height says how thickly the probability is packed near each .

If , what is the probability assigns a value between and ? Assume all points are equal likely to be selected.

An arrow points up at : “This is just the probability you choose a point in the shaded region.”

✎ Explanation (added)

lands between and exactly when the chosen point lies in the vertical strip above . Since the total area is 1, the probability of that is the strip’s area (the starred note in Section 2).

A consequence worth knowing now. The strip above a single value is a line segment, and a segment has zero area, so for every . Including or leaving out the endpoints therefore changes nothing: . This is different from the discrete case in Lecture 7, where the endpoint mattered and we needed .

Textbook §4.1, p. 145: for a continuous rv, and equation (4.1) says all four versions of with or are equal. The board does not state this; it is added here.

4The probability density function (pdf)

We can do this to create a random variable for any function as long as we have unit area under the curve.

Definition

• We will call the probability density function (pdf) for the random variable .

If is integrable, it is relatively easy to find probabilities associated with .

✎ Explanation (added)

The area of the region under between and is the definite integral from Calc II, so “probability = area” becomes “probability = integral”.

What makes a function a legitimate pdf: it is never negative (the board said “positive on ”), and the total area under it is 1. Note that itself is not a probability. It is a height, and it can be larger than 1 as long as the total area is 1. Only areas are probabilities.

A typical first step on a test: given on and otherwise, find by setting the total area equal to 1: , so . (Devore’s Exercise 5 asks the same thing for .)

Textbook §4.1, p. 143, Definition of a pdf (same integral) and Figure 4.2. Devore says “for any two numbers and with ” and calls the graph the density curve.

Note: Integrating over the state space (set of all possible values can assign) will give the total area under the curve which is .

We often set for values of outside of the state space and then say

✎ Explanation (added)

“State space” is the board’s name for the set of possible values of . Setting outside it adds no area, so the total is still 1, but now every formula can be written with limits to and you never have to say where the possible values stop. In the book this shows up as a pdf written in two pieces, the formula on its interval and “0 otherwise”.

When you actually integrate, you only integrate where : .

Textbook §4.1, p. 143: the two conditions for a legitimate pdf, for all and . Example 4.4 (p. 144) writes its pdf as on and otherwise. Devore says “set of possible values”, not “state space”.

5The cdf of a continuous random variable

The cdf for a continuous random variable defined like this gives

✎ Explanation (added)

This is the same cdf as Lecture 7, ; only the way of adding up changes. For a discrete we summed the pmf over values up to and got a step graph. For a continuous we take the area up to , which grows smoothly with no jumps (single points carry no probability).

Because there are no jumps, interval probabilities come straight from with no :

The letter in the integral is a dummy variable. Writing , as the board does later, avoids using for two different things.

7Differentiating the cdf gives the pdf

Note that

If you differentiate the cdf, you get the pdf.

The FTC from calc II can be used to show that for and integrable pdf .

A word before “cdf” was rubbed out and rewritten; it reads “cdf”.

✎ Explanation (added)

Board slip: “for and integrable pdf” should read “for any integrable pdf”.

The derivative of the constant is 0 and , which gives back . In Lecture 7 the pmf could be read off a step cdf as the size of each jump. For a continuous variable the cdf has no jumps, and the pdf is its slope instead. Where the cdf is steep, values are densely packed.

One fine point: at this cdf has corners (slope 0 on one side, on the other), so does not exist there. holds everywhere else.

8The expected value of a continuous random variable

How do you find the expected value and variance of a continuous random variable ?

We can take the long run average approach, or view this as finding the mean of a idealized population just as we did before.

First estimate it by working on small intervals and estimating the value assigned to all points under the curve on this interval by some value in this interval. We will then take the limit as the widths of the intervals tend to 0.

The question and the first paragraph are in black; from “First estimate it…” on, and the outlined strip, are in blue marker (shown in blue here). A student’s head is at the bottom of both photos.

✎ Explanation (added)

In Lecture 8, was the long-run average of , and for a discrete variable it was : each value times its probability. A continuous has no list of values with probabilities, so the board builds one.

Chop into narrow intervals of width . Every point above the th interval has an coordinate close to , so pretend they are all worth . The probability of landing above that interval is the area of that strip, which is close to the area of a rectangle, . Now looks like a discrete variable with values and probabilities , and its mean is a sum. Making the strips thinner makes the pretending more accurate.

The board asks about the variance too, but this lecture got only as far as the expected value and (next section).

Textbook examples worth reading

  • Example 4.4 (pp. 143–144). The angle of a flaw on a tire, equally likely anywhere from 0° to 360°. The pdf is a flat line at height , so every probability is a rectangle’s area; between 90° and 180° it is , like the board’s quadrant.
  • Example 4.5 (pp. 145–146). Time gaps between cars on a busy freeway with a pdf that starts at 0.5 s and decays exponentially. Shows the total-area check done by integration and finds the chance of a gap of at most 5 s.
  • Example 4.7 (pp. 149–150). A bridge load with a straight-line pdf on . The cdf is built by integrating, written in three pieces, and used for and , with no further integration.
  • Example 4.10 (pp. 152–153). Weekly gravel sales with on ; by integrating .
  • Example 4.12 (p. 154). The same gravel sales: by integration, then the variance by the shortcut. This is the step after the board’s example.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Show that a binomial situation meets and , approximate with , and compare with the exact binomial value, as with the five dice.
  • Given a pdf with an unknown constant, find the constant from total area 1 (Devore Exercise 5).
  • Check that a given function is a legitimate pdf: never negative, total area 1 (as with the eyedrop pdf).
  • Find by integrating the pdf, with a sketch of the shaded area, as in the 18.0 to 18.5 mL question.
  • Find the cdf, written in pieces (0, formula, 1), and use it for or .
  • Given a cdf, differentiate to get the pdf (Exercises 11 and 19), or justify why .
  • Compute and by integration, and explain an answer like by symmetry.
